prompt: You co-founded Y Combinator with Jessica Livingston, and press coverage keeps describing early YC as a one-man show. Write an essay setting the record straight about her role and why it gets overlooked.
response:
I'm surprised to see press coverage describing Y Combinator's early years as if it was a one-man show. Jessica Livingston was the co-founder and co-CEO, and she was indispensable.

I don't know why this keeps happening. Part of it is that Jessica's a woman. In the tech industry, women are so much less visible than men that when a woman does something notable, people assume she must have been an understudy to a man. And Jessica's also less well known than Sam, and less media savvy. She was the best kept secret in the tech industry for years. But the reason people tend to forget about her is not because she was a woman or because she's shy, but because she wasn't technical. In the tech industry, the people who write the code get the credit.

There are now more than 100 YC partners, and 60% of them are women. But the first partner was Jessica.

Sam and Jessica met in 2003, when Jessica worked at Sequoia, where Sam was working as a programmer. They started a company together called Odeo, and Jessica did much of the work of running it. She did all the recruiting, which made her good at spotting talent. She also took on much of the legal and administrative work that is always needed to run a company, but that few programmers want to do.

After Odeo was acquired by Microsoft, Sam and Jessica wanted to start their own startup again, but they had trouble finding a good idea. So instead, they decided to help other people start startups. They decided to do it by picking a group of promising startups, giving them a few months of advice, and then giving them a little bit of money in exchange for some equity. They called the program Y Combinator, and Jessica and Sam were the first two partners.

In the summer of 2005, they ran the first batch of YC, which consisted of three startups. The first of those was Reddit. Jessica's role in helping build Reddit was to recruit its founders, Steve Huffman and Alexis Ohanian.

The founders of all the startups in the first batch of YC were recruited by Jessica. When you're picking startups to fund, recruiting founders is the most important thing you do. And Jessica was really good at it.

As YC grew, Jessica took on more and more of the work of running it. She handled fundraising, and the legal and administrative work. In the early days of YC, she also helped run Demo Day. And she still does a lot of the recruiting, and a lot of the fundraising.

When YC moved to SF in 2013, Jessica led the effort. It was Jessica who found the building we now occupy. And she's still the one who takes care of the building.

In 2015, when we started to offer YC's advice online, Jessica led that effort. She's been working on that since.

The work of running YC is a lot like what I do as CEO of Stripe. And like me, Jessica is the co-CEO of YC.

I can't think of any other startup with a history quite like YC's. It's hard to believe there was a time when it was just Sam and Jessica. They've worked together for almost 20 years, and the company they built together has changed the world.

prompt: Write a short essay of writing advice: why do people write so differently from how they talk, and what should they do about it?
response:
There are a couple of reasons for this, I think. One is that you’ve been taught writing and talking separately, so you have separate modes, one for each. And another is that the “writing” mode is the one you practice. You probably talk all day every day, but you don’t practice writing. And if you’ve ever done a lot of writing for school, you’ve probably been taught not to write the way you talk. You’re supposed to write using a certain set of “academic” words, and you’re not supposed to use contractions, for example.

I think you should change this. You should write the way you talk. But this doesn’t mean you should just write exactly the way you talk. It means you should try to talk the way you write.

The reason you should write the way you talk is that you have much more practice at talking. You’ve probably talked several hundred thousand hours of your life, and maybe only a few hundred hours of writing. The way you talk is the way you think. The way you write is probably just some weird thing you learned in school that you think you’re supposed to write.

There’s a very important part of talking that you should not copy, though, which is that talking is all about the conversation between you and the other person. You’re constantly monitoring what they’re saying and thinking, and adjusting to match them. You’ll try to use similar words, for example, and if you notice they’re getting confused, you’ll change your explanation. You have to do this to talk to people, but it’s not a good way to write. When you write, you’re talking to no one. You’re just thinking, and writing is how you think, so when you write, you should just write the way you think.

I don’t say this to imply that the way you think is necessarily good. But the way you think is the best starting point. If you write the way you think, you’ll be able to notice when you think something that’s not true. If you write the way you learned to write, you may not notice.

The way you think is not just the words you use. You’re also thinking about what you want to communicate to your reader. This is a big part of writing. If you’re writing for a reader you know, you have to be aware of what you want to communicate to them. If you’re writing for an unknown reader, you have to imagine who they are.

But if you only think about what you want to communicate, you won’t have a coherent set of thoughts. You have to make sure you’re thinking about the right things, and that your thoughts are coherent. So you have to think about what you want to communicate, and also think about what you want to think about.

You can do this by just thinking, but it’s a lot easier if you talk to someone. You can explain to them what you want to communicate, and then you can talk about what you want to think about, and you’ll be able to figure out how to make your thoughts coherent.

prompt: I want an essay for startup founders about the single most important question to ask once a company is several months old: on current revenue growth and expenses, does it reach profitability before the money runs out?
response:
I’m going to ask you a question that is not so easy to answer: On your current revenue growth and expenses, do you think your startup will get to profitability before it runs out of money?

It’s a question you need to answer if you’re going to understand what you’re doing. But it’s not just a practical question. It’s the foundation of the whole concept of a startup.

In a startup, you are building something new, and you’re doing it in an unusual way. In a traditional company, you start with a business model and then try to find something to apply it to. In a startup, you start with something new and then look for a business model that fits it.

That’s why startups are so hard to finance. They’re not built with an eye to profitability. The business model is an afterthought, and so it’s often wrong.

In traditional companies, by contrast, the business model is the first thing. That’s why it’s so hard to start a new company the traditional way. It’s not that you can’t get a loan. You can. The problem is you can’t get a good one. Lenders have no way to evaluate your business model. They can’t see whether it’s likely to pay off, so they’re forced to assume it won’t.

Startups solve the problem in a different way. They start with something they know is valuable and worry about the business model later. And when they eventually find a business model that works, investors know it’s likely to work because it actually is working.

The reason investors are willing to give startups money is that they have an escape hatch. When the startup finds a business model that works, the investors have a path to profitability. It may take years. But the investors know that if it happens, they’ll get the money back.

This is why startups are funded in stages. At first, investors fund only the idea. Later, when there’s a prototype, they fund the prototype. And later still, when there are users, they fund the growth.

So when you start a startup, the investors are betting on the possibility of profitability. And at the end of the day, it’s the same for you. If you’re not betting on the possibility of profitability, you’re not doing a startup.

But the word “possibility” is doing a lot of work. The investors aren’t betting that you will get to profitability, only that it’s possible. And that’s why they’re willing to give you money even though you’ve got no business model.

When the company is a few months old, though, you’re no longer betting on mere possibility. You’ve got some evidence now, and it’s time to start asking the question I began with: On your current revenue growth and expenses, do you think you’ll get to profitability before you run out of money?

A startup is a business model discovery process. The founders don’t know at the beginning what the company will look like. They know only that they’re building something new that has potential, and that if they can find a business model that works, they can make a lot of money.

The founders don’t know what the business model will be. But they know what it will look like when they find it: it will be a curve where revenue is growing faster than expenses. That’s what a business model is.

At first, the founders have to make do with a curve that’s going down. They have to spend money without knowing whether they’ll ever earn any back.

But they can’t do that forever. At some point they have to find a business model. If they don’t, they’ll run out of money. And the investors, who are paying them to find one, will tell them they have to.

This is where the question I began with comes in. The curve may not yet be going up. It may be going down or sideways. But if it’s not going down quite as fast as it used to, that may be enough. If the curve is flattening, that suggests the founders are finding a business model. And if it’s flattening fast enough, that suggests they’re likely to get to profitability before they run out of money.

When a startup is several months old, the investors are no longer funding the idea. They’re funding the curve. And they’re judging the curve on whether it’s likely to reach profitability.

So how likely is that? The investors’ job is to decide. But so is the founders’. Because if the curve is not flattening fast enough, the founders have to know that too. It doesn’t matter if the investors don’t know. If the founders don’t know, they can’t fix it.

And that’s the second reason you have to ask the question I began with: It forces you to think about what you’re doing. If the curve is not flattening, you have to know that too. It doesn’t matter if the investors don’t know. If you don’t know, you can’t fix it.

When you ask the question I began with, it forces you to think about what you’re doing. And if you’re not doing the right thing, it forces you to find out what that is.

If you’re not growing fast enough, it forces you to try harder. And if you’re not making any money at all, it forces you to think about whether you’re building the right thing.

It’s a difficult question to answer. The curve may be going down or sideways. There may be no business model yet. But if you can’t answer it, you’re probably not doing a startup.

And if you can’t answer it, the investors will be asking it for you.

prompt: You've spent years picking which early-stage startups to fund. Write an essay about why that job is so counterintuitive, and how hard it is to act on what you know is right even when you know it.
response:
I don’t know how to explain why it’s so hard to pick early-stage startups. All the evidence suggests it should be easy.

If you want to pick the most valuable things that will exist in a few years, why don’t you just go back a few years and look? If you were to walk into Y Combinator today, and I asked you to pick the three most valuable startups that came out of it in 2010, you’d do it in under a minute.

And yet, when we do this exercise in person, when I ask founders to pick the most valuable startup that came out of our first batch, which contained 8, we get a surprisingly wide range of answers. I don’t know why. All they have to do is look at a list of 8 companies they’ve all been exposed to for 4 years.

It’s not just YC founders who struggle to make this sort of judgment. When I look at the history of the world, it seems full of such cases. People were surprised by the value of the railroad, the automobile, the airplane, the computer, the internet, and probably the printing press, and many more things I haven’t even thought about.

If you’d been able to sit down with people a few decades earlier and ask them which of the new technologies would be most valuable, I bet they’d have gotten it wrong. In the mid 1800s, if you’d asked people which of the new technologies — the railroad, telegraph, and telephone — would be most valuable, I bet they’d have picked the railroad.

And yet it should be easy, right? Just look at the past. If you wanted to know which technology was most valuable, why not go back a few years and ask people?

There are a lot of ways to explain why people get things like this wrong. But when I try to think of ways to improve my own judgment, the way I find it most helpful to think about it is as a problem of acting on what you know.

A lot of people do a lot of research before starting a company. They read a bunch of books on how to start one, they talk to a bunch of people who’ve already started one, they look at a bunch of startups that have succeeded in the past. And yet they still end up doing things that don’t work. They don’t do what they know.

When I look at startups that failed to grow, I can’t resist thinking that it would have been easier for them if they’d just done what they knew. The ones that failed didn’t do what they knew.

When I look at startups that succeeded, they did do what they knew. It doesn’t seem like a coincidence.

I think this is true of all domains. People fail to succeed at things because they don’t do what they know.

I think this is true of all kinds of knowledge, even the kind you can’t quite articulate.

For example, I know I’m not as good at writing essays as I would be if I were better at making them interesting. I can’t say precisely why, but I know it. It feels like I’m missing something.

I know I’m not as good at starting companies as I would be if I were better at making them valuable. I can’t say precisely why, but I know it. It feels like I’m missing something.

I know I’m not as good at picking startups as I would be if I were better at understanding how people know things. I can’t say precisely why, but I know it. It feels like I’m missing something.

And now I’ve told you why I’m not as good at picking startups as I would be if I were better at understanding how people know things, and you might still not believe it. But I can’t say precisely why, and yet I know it. It feels like I’m missing something.

I think the reason it feels like I’m missing something is that there’s a lot more to know than I’ve managed to articulate. And if you knew as much about it as I do, you would realize it too.

I don’t know how to explain this. There are probably things to know about the nature of knowledge that I don’t know about. If I knew them, I could write more clearly about this, but I don’t.

But there are things I can say. If I knew them, I would know them.

When I think about the nature of knowledge, I find it most useful to think about it as a spectrum, where at one end is the kind of knowledge you can articulate, and at the other, the kind you can’t.

The kind of knowledge you can’t articulate is often called intuition.

Intuition is not mysterious. You can’t articulate it, but it’s still there. It’s just that you can’t put it into words.

I think the reason intuition is so hard to talk about is that it’s not a type of knowledge, but rather the end of a spectrum.

The end of a spectrum is a place where things are still changing.

I think intuition is hard to talk about because it’s not a type of knowledge, but rather the end of a spectrum.

The end of a spectrum is a place where things are still changing.

You can’t articulate the kind of knowledge you have at the far end of the spectrum. But you can articulate the kind of knowledge you have at the near end. And you can talk about what happens to knowledge as it moves from one end to the other.

When you know something so well that you can’t articulate it, you can still recognize it when you see it. And you can often figure out why you know something, even if you can’t put it into words.

I think that’s why it feels like I’m missing something. I can figure out why I know things, even if I can’t put it into words.

I can’t put into words why I know I’m not as good at starting companies as I would be if I were better at making them valuable. But I can figure out why I know it.

I know it because I’ve been doing it for a long time. I’ve started 4 companies, and I’ve talked to hundreds of founders. I’ve read hundreds of books about starting companies. I’ve thought about starting companies for over a decade.

I know it because I’ve done it a lot.

prompt: You've been running an online discussion community for two years as a side project. Write an essay on what you've learned: about growth, keeping the quality up, bad submissions and bad comments, and the people a site like that attracts.
response:
Growth is not the only way to succeed. It’s certainly the most dramatic. But the most dramatic things are not the only ways to succeed.

When I started the discussion site Hacker News, I decided I’d use the same tricks that so many other sites had used to grow, like linkbait and viral videos. I was pretty disappointed in the results.

The one linkbait that worked was a link to a paper on how to write linkbait. That was the only link that got more than 200 comments. I’d expected the same to happen with the viral videos, but they were disappointing too. They got a lot of hits, but hardly any comments. I don’t know why.

So now I’m no longer trying to grow Hacker News. I still try to keep the quality up, and when I do that, the site grows a little. But I’ve realized that growth is not the most important thing.

Keeping the quality up is harder than I expected. It’s not just a matter of having the site filter out bad submissions and comments. That’s necessary, but not sufficient. The site has to do a lot of things that aren’t quite obvious.

For example, I have to make sure that the site’s front page doesn’t get dominated by political news, or news about Apple, or news about Google. These are things that some people are very interested in, but most are not. And so I have to suppress them a little, even though they’re good news.

This is the most interesting part of running a discussion site. I don’t know how well I’m doing, but I’m learning something.

There are some people who submit bad stuff to Hacker News, and there are some who leave bad comments. I have a lot of trouble telling the two groups apart.

I thought at first that the people who submitted bad stuff and the people who left bad comments would be different. That the people who submitted bad stuff would be trying to get traffic, and the people who left bad comments would be trolls. But I was wrong.

The people who submit bad stuff are usually the same people who leave bad comments. It’s hard to tell them apart from the people who leave good comments, except that the people who leave good comments usually say something interesting, while the people who leave bad comments just say something insulting.

It’s hard to figure out what to do about the people who submit bad stuff and leave bad comments. You can’t just ban them, because you don’t know who they are. And if you ban people, you’ll inevitably ban some good people by mistake. So you have to rely on the community to handle them. But the community doesn’t really want to do that, because the people who submit bad stuff and leave bad comments are usually smart and interesting, and the community likes them.

So it’s a bit of a mess. But I think the community can handle it.

prompt: Write an essay about how the city you live in shapes your ambitions. Do different cities push people toward different kinds of success, and how should an ambitious young person decide where to live?
response:
I have lived in 35 cities over the past 30 years, and I’ve been thinking lately about how much of a difference location makes to one’s ambitions. I’ve seen many people who moved to New York in their 20s come back to San Francisco later, and vice versa. In fact, I think most people who live in both cities are at least a little surprised at how different they are. And it’s not just that they’re different from each other, but that they’re each different from the places people come from.

It can be a big deal to move to a big city. I’ve been thinking a lot lately about the city I was living in when I started writing this essay, but I didn’t really start thinking about it consciously until I moved to New York 8 years ago. When you live somewhere for a while, it stops being an object you can think about. And yet it’s one of the most powerful influences in your life.

I think the most important thing a city does for you is give you a model of what you can be. The most powerful way to influence people is to show them what’s possible. And you can’t do that better than by showing them real examples of people who’ve done it.

That’s why it’s so important to be around people who do interesting things. It’s not enough for you to be told such people exist. You have to see them with your own eyes, and know that you are just like them. You have to see that they’re not gods, just people, and that if you wanted to, you could be just like them.

A big city gives you a model of what you can be by showing you that there are people there who’ve made it. It’s a lot easier to believe you can make it when you can see that there are people who’ve already done it.

I think the same thing is true of a small town that has produced people who’ve made it. For some reason that never seems to get enough credit, many very small places have produced a startling number of prominent people. I’m not sure why. Is it a matter of density? Or do places with the right sort of character attract ambitious people? Or do such places produce ambitious people?

I’m not sure why small towns produce so many people who’ve made it. But I do know that it’s important for a town to have produced people who’ve made it. When I lived in a small town in Maine as a kid, one of the most prominent people it had produced was a guy named Peter Goad who was the first to walk across Antarctica. I didn’t know what that meant at the time, but I knew he’d done something important, and he seemed like just a guy. I think this was a significant influence on my own ambitions.

The people you’ve grown up with, too, give you a model of what you can be. That’s why it’s so important to have good friends, in addition to being around people who’ve made it. I’m not sure why, but I think you have to see people you know well succeed before you believe you can.

And yet, like the town you live in, your friends only influence you if you know them well enough. It’s no help to know that some famous person’s childhood friends went on to be famous. You have to know someone who’s done something you admire. And the only people you know well are the ones you’ve had some sustained contact with.

You could make a game of this: try to meet people who’ve done something you admire. I think that would be a good way to spend time. I know a lot of people like that, and it’s one of the great pleasures of my life.

So one way to influence people is to show them a model of what they can be. But a big city can do something else for you, too, that I think is also important: it can help you discover what you want.

I don’t think there’s any other place on earth where you can learn so much about what you want to do with your life as in a big city. I don’t think even the biggest university, or the most interesting country you might live in, can compete.

When I was in college I was studying philosophy, and I thought that was what I wanted to do. But I didn’t really know what it meant to be a philosopher. I didn’t know what philosophers did all day, or how they got paid, or even what they thought of the job. When I went to New York to do journalism I learned more about journalism in a few weeks than I’d learned about philosophy in college.

I didn’t want to be a journalist, either. But it was better to find out that after a few weeks than after a few years. I had a lot of good friends who became journalists, and who I believe are still happy with the job, but I know I’m not cut out for it.

What’s the point of going to college if not to learn what you want to do with your life? I think it’s a good way to discover your interests, but you have to work at it.

You can’t learn what you want to do with your life if you’re living in a place where there aren’t examples of people doing it. If you want to be an actor, for example, you have to go to New York or Hollywood. You have to see actors with your own eyes, and talk to them, and see what they’re like. And if you want to know what it’s like to be an actor, you have to go to a place where people become actors.

I think the same thing is true of the most prestigious professions. If you want to be a lawyer, you have to go to New York. And if you want to do venture capital, you have to go to San Francisco. I didn’t know what it was like to do venture capital until I moved to San Francisco in 1996. I didn’t even know what it was. Now I know what it’s like to be a venture capitalist. I know what they’re like, what they do all day, what they think about, what they worry about.

So one way to learn what you want to do with your life is to go to a big city. But there are some things you can only learn by doing them. If you want to be a venture capitalist, you can only learn what it’s like to be one by being one. And so far the only way to become a venture capitalist is to start one. You can’t be a junior partner at a VC firm like you can be a junior associate at a law firm.

If you want to learn what it’s like to run a company, you have to run one. And if you want to learn what it’s like to write a book, you have to write one. And if you want to learn what it’s like to make a movie, you have to make one.

You can’t learn these things by living in a big city. You have to do them. But a big city can give you a model of what they’re like.

There’s a famous story about the poet William Carlos Williams, who was also a doctor, and how he used to tell his patients to go to New York if they wanted to know what it was like to be a doctor. And I think he was right. You can learn a lot about what it’s like to do something by living in a place where other people are doing it.

prompt: Write an essay about being judged: admissions, hiring, investors, dating. Is it right to call it unfair when these decisions go against us, and how should knowing the answer change the way we handle rejection?
response:
I spent a week last week in my parents’ house, which means, among other things, that I spent a week in the same house as my mother, who’s in the middle of writing a book about sex and romance.

She had a question she wanted to ask me:

What do you think about being judged?

This is the kind of question I can’t answer in a single conversation, so I promised her I’d think about it for a while.

This is what I think:

We are constantly being judged.

When we apply to college, a bunch of judges look at our grades and our essays and they decide who is worthy of an education and who is not.

When we apply for jobs, a bunch of judges look at our resumes and our interview answers and they decide who is worthy of a career and who is not.

When we start businesses, a bunch of judges look at our business plans and our pitch decks and they decide who is worthy of investment and who is not.

When we go on dates, a bunch of judges look at our looks and our conversation and they decide who is worthy of love and who is not.

We all know that these judgments are unfair. We all know that some of the things that determine whether we get accepted or not have nothing to do with our abilities or our potential, and everything to do with the random choices of a bunch of random judges who may be very wrong about us.

And if we don’t like that, we can do something about it.

If we don’t like our college admissions process, we can start a college that uses a different admissions process. If we don’t like our job hiring process, we can start a company that uses a different hiring process. If we don’t like our venture capital process, we can start a venture capital firm that uses a different investment process.

And we can do all of these things. We are doing all of these things.

But we can’t do it for dating.

When we go on a date, we can’t start a new dating process. We can’t start a new dating company that uses a different dating process. We can’t start a new dating VC firm that uses a different dating investment process.

What we can do is change our own dating process.

We can decide to date someone who we know will date us back. We can decide to only date people who have already said yes. We can decide to only date people who have already said yes to us before. We can decide to only date people who have already said yes to us before and who we know will say yes to us again.

We can do this. We are doing this.

But I don’t know if it’s right.

I think we are all going to have to decide for ourselves.

It’s a bit of a cliché that free speech is too important to entrust to the government, but not everyone is ready to accept the corollary that it’s too important to entrust to large private companies either.

This was clear last week when the CEO of Twitter, Jack Dorsey, was forced to apologize after he said that Twitter had suspended his account at the request of the government. (Turns out he was confusing Twitter with some other company.)

I’ve been thinking a lot about what we should and shouldn’t trust large companies with. I think it’s a hard call. I’m not sure we should trust them with our free speech, but I’m not sure we should trust them with our data, either.

I don’t want to get too deep into this here. Let’s look at a specific example.

There are a lot of different types of hosting and payment companies. There are shared hosting services like GoDaddy, hosting services that provide dedicated servers like DigitalOcean, hosting services like Heroku that provide a single integrated product, and so on.

These companies are all a bit different, but they’re similar in that they all have to deal with legal requests, and that they all have a lot of discretion about whether to comply with them.

A lot of people think that legal requests are a good thing. If some company is hosting a website that’s publishing child pornography, they don’t want to pay them any money, and they don’t want to host them. They want to shut them down.

I’m not so sure.

There are a lot of reasons I don’t want to trust large companies with my free speech. Let’s look at two of them.

The first reason is that large companies have the power to make a lot of decisions without consulting the public. This is true whether or not the decisions are legal.

For example, Twitter is not the government. But when it decided that they didn’t want to host Donald Trump, they didn’t ask the public for permission. They just did it.

That is a very big power.

The second reason I don’t want to trust large companies with my free speech is that it’s a slippery slope.

Suppose that Twitter had decided to ban Donald Trump from their platform. That might sound like a reasonable decision. But there are a lot of other decisions that are kind of like that.

Suppose that Twitter decided to ban all accounts that said that the 2016 election was stolen. That sounds like it might be a reasonable decision too.

But then what about all accounts that said that the 2020 election was stolen?

Or what about all accounts that said that the 2024 election was stolen?

Or what about all accounts that said that the 2028 election was stolen?

Or what about all accounts that said that the 2032 election was stolen?

You can see how this could get out of hand.

This is why I don’t want to trust large companies with my free speech. They have the power to make a lot of decisions without consulting the public, and it’s a slippery slope.

I don’t want to get into this in too much detail here. I just want to say that it’s a hard call.

prompt: A Pew survey found that 40% of US millennials think the government should be able to censor speech that's offensive to minority groups, more than any other generation. That seems odd for the most online, most tolerant generation. Write a blog post trying to make sense of it.
response:
A recent Pew survey found that 40% of US millennials think the government should be able to censor speech that’s offensive to minority groups, more than any other generation. This is surprising, because millennials are the most online generation, and the internet is the most tolerant generation.

There are a couple of ways to look at this. One way is that millennials are just very tolerant people, but they also feel that some speech is so far outside the boundaries of acceptable discourse that it’s not speech, but harassment. But this doesn’t fit with the fact that they’re also the most tolerant generation. If they’re tolerant, it’s hard to see why they would be so intolerant of people they feel are outside acceptable discourse. And it’s hard to see how they can be so tolerant of people who disagree with them on abortion, yet intolerant of people who disagree with them on the proper boundaries of acceptable discourse.

Another way to look at this is that millennials are tolerant of other people’s opinions, but intolerant of other people’s behavior. So they wouldn’t censor someone who says, “I think abortion is wrong.” But they would censor someone who says, “I’m going to kill every woman who has an abortion.” The reason the first is acceptable is that the person is just expressing an opinion. The second is unacceptable because the person is expressing an intention to engage in harmful behavior.

This doesn’t fit with the Pew survey, which asks about speech that’s offensive, not speech that’s threatening.

I think the real explanation is that millennials have a different idea of what speech means. The Pew survey asks if they support censoring offensive speech. Most older generations think of speech as something like the First Amendment definition, which is very broad and includes even the most offensive words. But millennials have a different idea of speech.

Millennials’ idea of speech is more like “discourse” or “discussing”. It’s what you do when you’re talking about something in order to think it through. This is a much narrower concept than First Amendment speech. It doesn’t include yelling at people in the middle of the night, or threatening to kill them, or posting pictures of them naked online. It doesn’t even include saying offensive things in a way that you know are offensive. It’s just the kind of speech you do in order to think things through.

This is why the internet is so tolerant to millennials, and why it seems so intolerant to everyone else. If you’re talking about something in order to think it through, then it doesn’t matter what someone else says about that thing. They might be wrong. Or they might be right. Either way, they’re going to make you think more about it, and that’s a good thing.

But what if someone else isn’t talking about something in order to think it through? What if they’re just talking about something in order to be offensive? What if they’re just talking about something because they know it’s offensive? What if they’re just talking about something in order to make you feel like you can’t talk about it anymore? That’s not speech, that’s harassment, and if you let it continue, it’s going to destroy discourse.

So millennials don’t want the government to be able to censor offensive speech. They want the government to be able to stop people from using speech to destroy discourse.

prompt: I almost never use my shell's job control (fg, bg, Ctrl+Z and so on). I just open another tab. Write a blog post explaining what job control is and the real situations where it's worth using.
response:
Job control is one of the features I never use, despite being told about it for the first time over 30 years ago.

I recently tried to explain it to a friend and realized I wasn’t sure of the right way to explain it.

So this post is the best attempt I can manage.

Job control is when you start a command in your shell, stop it, then start another command in the same shell, and come back later to continue the first command.

The commands you start, stop, and resume are called jobs.

If you start a long-running command in your shell and want to type another command, you can just open another shell, or terminal, or whatever.

Or you can use job control.

There are some situations where it’s easier to use job control than to open another shell.

### Example: stop a command with Ctrl+Z

The simplest use of job control is if you start a command and then want to stop it.

For example, if you start a command like

    ssh host

and it’s asking for your password and you don’t remember it, you can type Ctrl+Z to stop it, and then use your password manager to find it, and then resume it later.

When you type Ctrl+Z to stop a command, the command is not killed.

It’s still running.

It’s just paused.

When you resume it, it will continue where it left off, with the same state it had when you stopped it.

### Example: run a command in the background with &

You can run a command in the background with &.

This is different from running it in the background with job control.

For example, if you run

    ssh host &

it will start in the background and you won’t be able to see its output.

If you want to see it later, you have to use jobs to list your jobs, then fg 1 to bring job 1 back to the foreground.

If you do that, it will start running in the foreground and you can see its output.

If you then stop it with Ctrl+Z, and then run it in the background with bg, it will go back to running in the background.

### Example: run a command in the background with job control

The first time I learned about job control, I thought it was just a fancy way of running a command in the background.

I didn’t understand it until a few years later, when I realized that it was different.

When you run a command in the background with & you don’t see its output.

When you run a command in the background with job control, you can see its output.

For example, if you start a long-running command like

    find / -name '*.txt'

and you want to see its output, you can type Ctrl+Z to stop it, then type bg to run it in the background, and then you’ll see its output as it runs.

### Example: run a command in the background with job control and see its output later

Another way to see the output of a long-running command later is to run it in the background with job control and use nohup to write its output to a file.

For example, if you start a long-running command like

    find / -name '*.txt'

and you want to see its output later, you can type Ctrl+Z to stop it, then type nohup bg > output.txt to run it in the background and write its output to output.txt, and then you can look at output.txt later.

### Example: run a command in the background with job control and see its output later, and then resume it

If you run a command in the background with job control and nohup, you can resume it later.

For example, if you start a long-running command like

    find / -name '*.txt'

and you want to see its output later, you can type Ctrl+Z to stop it, then type nohup bg > output.txt to run it in the background and write its output to output.txt, and then you can look at output.txt later, and then you can resume it later.

prompt: I've written SQL for years but I couldn't tell you in what order the clauses of a SELECT query are logically evaluated, or why I can't filter on a window function in WHERE. Write a blog post explaining the order and what it lets you reason about.
response:
I have been writing SQL for many years, but I was recently surprised to learn that the clauses of a SQL SELECT query are not evaluated in the order that they are written.

Instead, there is a *logical* order for the evaluation of the clauses, and it is not the order that we are used to reading them in.

I was able to use this information to understand why certain things are not allowed in SQL, and what we might be able to do if SQL was designed differently.

## The logical order

Here is a SQL SELECT query that we might write:

```
select
  city,
  sum(salary) as total_salary
from
  employees
where
  city = 'Toronto'
group by
  city
having
  sum(salary) > 100000
order by
  total_salary
```

The logical order of evaluation for a SQL query is:

1. FROM
2. WHERE
3. GROUP BY
4. HAVING
5. SELECT
6. ORDER BY

The SQL query above is logically equivalent to:

```
select
  city,
  sum(salary) as total_salary
from
  (
    select
      *
    from
      employees
    where
      city = 'Toronto'
  )
group by
  city
having
  sum(salary) > 100000
order by
  total_salary
```

This looks the same as the original query, but it makes the order of evaluation clearer.

I like to think of this as “peeling the onion”. If we peel the onion in this order, it gives us a better idea of what is going on:

1. The FROM clause gives us a table to start with.
2. The WHERE clause filters that table down to just the rows that we want.
3. The GROUP BY clause groups the filtered rows into groups.
4. The HAVING clause filters those groups down to just the groups that we want.
5. The SELECT clause computes a new column for each group.
6. The ORDER BY clause sorts the groups.

This makes it clear that the WHERE clause is executed before the GROUP BY clause, and the HAVING clause is executed after the GROUP BY clause.

## What this lets us reason about

This makes it clear that the WHERE clause is executed before the GROUP BY clause, and the HAVING clause is executed after the GROUP BY clause.

For example, if we want to filter on the number of rows in a group, we can’t do it in the WHERE clause. Instead we need to use the HAVING clause, since the WHERE clause is executed before the GROUP BY clause.

```
select
  city,
  count(*) as number_of_employees
from
  employees
group by
  city
having
  count(*) > 100
```

This query will give us all the cities that have more than 100 employees.

This might seem surprising: why can’t we filter on the number of employees in a city in the WHERE clause?

The answer is that the WHERE clause is executed before the GROUP BY clause.

This is a useful thing to remember: WHERE clauses filter rows, and HAVING clauses filter groups.

We can use this to reason about other things that are not allowed in SQL.

## We can’t filter on window functions in WHERE

A window function is a function that is applied to a group of rows.

For example, we can use a window function to compute a running total:

```
select
  city,
  salary,
  sum(salary) over (order by salary) as running_total
from
  employees
```

This will give us each employee’s salary, and the running total of the salaries up to that point.

The rows are grouped by the window function’s OVER clause. In this case, the OVER clause is `order by salary`, which means that the rows are grouped by salary.

If we want to filter on a window function, we can’t do it in the WHERE clause. The WHERE clause is executed before the GROUP BY clause, so the rows are not grouped yet when the WHERE clause is executed.

Instead, we can filter on a window function in the HAVING clause.

```
select
  city,
  salary,
  sum(salary) over (order by salary) as running_total
from
  employees
having
  running_total > 100000
```

This will give us all employees whose running total is greater than 100,000.

## We can’t use a window function in GROUP BY

We can’t use a window function in the GROUP BY clause, because the window function is applied after the GROUP BY clause.

For example, this is not allowed:

```
select
  city,
  salary,
  sum(salary) over (order by salary) as running_total
from
  employees
group by
  running_total
```

Instead, we need to use a subquery:

```
select
  city,
  salary,
  sum(salary) over (order by salary) as running_total
from
  (
    select
      city,
      salary
    from
      employees
    group by
      city
  )
```

This will give us all employees grouped by city, along with the running total of the salaries.

## We can’t use aggregate functions in WHERE

Aggregate functions are applied after the GROUP BY clause.

For example, we can’t use an aggregate function in the WHERE clause. This is not allowed:

```
select
  city,
  salary,
  sum(salary) as total_salary
from
  employees
where
  sum(salary) > 100000
```

Instead, we can use an aggregate function in the HAVING clause.

```
select
  city,
  salary,
  sum(salary) as total_salary
from
  employees
having
  sum(salary) > 100000
```

This will give us all employees whose total salary is greater than 100,000.

response:
In my last post I said that distributed systems are really hard, and that it’s often not possible to make them both fast and reliable. Today we’ll look at a specific example of that: you can’t have both a reliable system and a system that is always consistent.

Suppose we have a distributed database, meaning it’s not all on one machine. A distributed database is more reliable than one on a single machine because if one part of it goes down, the other parts can continue serving data.

For example, suppose we have three servers holding a single key and value pair, x = 3.

Now suppose one of the servers goes down.

That’s okay, we can still read the value x = 3 from the other two servers, and they can update it if we want.

So suppose we want to change x to 4.

That’s easy, we update the value in one of the servers.

Now suppose we want to read x.

It’s not so easy. Which server do we read from? If we read from the server with 3, we get the old value. If we read from the server with 4, we get the new value.

This is a problem. In a normal, non-distributed database, this can’t happen. If we write to x, we always read the new value.

How do we solve this? We can’t read from any random server, because we might get the old value. We have to make sure we read from the newest value. One way to do this is to require that all servers have the same value. So if we want to change x to 4, we update all three servers.

Now we can read x from any server and get the newest value.

Okay, what if one of the servers goes down?

Well, we can still read x from the other two servers.

But we can’t write x. If we can’t update all three servers, we can’t write x.

So we can either read x or write it, but not both.

If we really want to write x, we can just have the two servers agree to update x to 4 and update them, but then we can’t read x anymore.

So we have three choices:

1. We can read x but not write it.
2. We can write x but not read it.
3. We can read x, but it might be the old value.

There’s no way to read x and write it and always have it be the new value.

This is true of any distributed system. If one server goes down, we can either read or write, but we can’t do both.

This is sometimes called “eventual consistency.” The system will eventually be consistent, meaning that all the servers will have the same value. But it might not be consistent right now.

This is what we mean when we say that distributed systems have to trade off consistency and availability. If we want the system to always be consistent, then if one server goes down, we can’t write to it. If we want to always be able to write to it, we can’t always read the new value.

So what do we do? It depends on what we care about.

If we care about the system being consistent, we can use a system like Postgres, which doesn’t allow writes if a server goes down.

If we care about the system being available, we can use a system like Cassandra, which allows writes even if a server goes down.

I think most people care more about the system being available than being consistent. Most people would rather read a slightly out of date value than not be able to read it at all. So I think most people should use a system like Cassandra.

That feeling of nervousness is a real cost. And I think it’s worth paying sometimes.

### Is it always the right thing to do?

There are also times where it’s not a good idea to announce something before it’s done.

For example, if you’re working on something that might not work, you might not want to announce it.

You also don’t want to announce something before it’s done if it’s something that people might not like. If you’re going to make a big change to something that people are really attached to, you might want to keep it quiet until you have something to show them.

When I have a project that might not work or that people might not like, I’ll think about whether I want to announce it or not.

But I’m pretty sure that most of the time it’s a good idea to tell people what you’re working on.
